messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 51
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: School Principal
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening illness
- Pcl5: 56

Three years ago, Marcus collapses during a parent-teacher conference. By the time he awakens in the ICU, the diagnosis is acute myocardial infarction with cardiogenic shock. He does not remember the fall as a single moment, but rather as a series of intrusions that still arrive unbidden. When he passes a hospital parking lot on his way to district meetings, his breath catches. He stops the car, grips the wheel, and waits until his heart rate drops. Paramedics who pull him from the gymnasium floor surface during staff training, superimposed over his teachers. After he returns to the administration building, he cannot step foot inside the campus clinic. The truth lives in the small things: the way he cancels mandatory wellness checks, the way he scans every staff meeting for unsteady breathing. He delegates less now. When a teacher coughs, Marcus excuses himself. He reads the district’s health bulletins twice, then deletes them without filing. Sleep has become a negotiation. He counts ceiling cracks until four in the morning, listening for the phantom hum of cardiac monitors. When his neighbor’s air conditioner kicks on, he is already awake, pulse hammering. He stops answering calls after nine p.m., telling himself it is grading season, though the silence is a wall against the possibility of a flatline. His widowhood compounds the quiet. His wife, Elena, dies two years later from a sudden aneurysm. Now, his grief sits beside the terror like two heavy stones in the same pocket. He goes through the motions of principalship—signing attendance sheets, nodding through budget reviews—but his mind drifts to the space between a heartbeat and the next. He catches himself monitoring his pulse during faculty luncheons. He avoids the gymnasium where he collapsed. He tells his assistant principal to handle the spring emergency drill alone. When forced to walk past the maintenance stairwell, he routes himself through the main lobby, even if it costs him ten minutes he cannot afford. In our sessions, Marcus speaks in careful paragraphs, as if structuring a board report. But the architecture of his avoidance shows in the margins. He checks his watch every time I mention the word clinic. He keeps his jacket buttoned even when the room is warm. He describes a recent incident: a sophomore faints during chemistry lab, and Marcus stands frozen in the doorway, hands trembling, until another teacher grabs the first-aid kit. Later, he tells me he apologizes to the parents, though what he omits is that he spends the afternoon in his office, convinced the floor would tilt again. He does not cry. He catalogs details instead—the scuff marks on the linoleum, the exact pitch of the alarm. He trusts data more than feeling now. We pause as the afternoon light shifts across his desk. Marcus unclasps his hands, rubs his thumb over his wedding ring, and looks out at the empty football field. He breathes in, holds it, and lets it out. The school day will begin again tomorrow. He will unlock the doors, greet the crossing guards, and sign the attendance ledger. He will try, as he always does, to stand in the space between what happened and what might happen next.
